posts.author: Seventh Son
posts.content_md:
I am proposing something that I believe would help this DCG forum. I think a universal standardized process would be to everyone’s benefit. None of us will ever be speaking the same (DCG) language if we don’t share certain constants. I realize that there is a host of reasons why everyone does their processes differently (gelatin, lasers, development). In my brief time on this forum I have experienced a great deal of frustration with the multitude of comments that bring little more than confusion to the individuals receiving them (mine included). 

I believe that the first BIG variable to be tackled is the *GELATIN* that we use. I have read a lot of cavalier comments about which type to use, and where to get it. But I guarantee that if my viscosity and bloom is different from what you are using, then virtually any advice I dispense will be of limited value. 

For example, if we’ve agreed to formulate 10-20-100, what have we really done? My gelatin is from Mars, and yours is from Venus. We think we’ve mixed the same 10grams of gelatin. But have we?

Because of the expense, I can’t imagine how we can unify the Laser portion of this problem. However, if we lock down the gelatin, and then agree upon a formula we will be dramatically closer to speaking the same language. Along with formula, a standardized developing process can be adopted.

How about we buy a communal barrel or two of gelatin?

I’m leaving a lot out, but I wanted to get some reaction before blathering on.

*United we stand, divided we fall.-Aesop*

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I think that to use a standard gelatin is a great idea. I would like to join on that.

But I think that the notation 10-20-100 is not sufficient for specification of DCG. Temperature and humidity should surely be included. I am not sure about classic DCG, but with MBDCG temperature and humidity play a very big role. I think there should be introduced a standard atmospheric condition. For example 25C and 65% humidity. And a standard drying time. Only then can we assure compatibility of results.

Humidity is not at all very difficult to control. Nowadays humidity controllers with accurate hygrostats can be bought for around 100 Euro.

Hey Guys,

Been away but now I'm back.

Really like this idea and hate it when someone throws a wet blanket on anything that promotes cooperation and standardization but here I go anyway Please take this as a point of discussion and cooperation and not me foo foo'ing an excellent idea.

It seems that gelatin is one factor of many (as info pointed out) and even with bloom strength there are factors within factors, such as film thickness, temperatures and coating methods. It would be like agreeing on a food receipe in which we all agree to use the same type of pasta but not look at the rest of the process. 

Seventh Son what is the main goal here? Is it that everyone makes DCG film the same and sees what happens? And what is the end result? Brighter, less whitening? Is it to sperate other variables such as post exposure or processing? I am guessing you are saying that we take one variable away and say this is the standard, but then what? Lastly, I think as important as standazation of gelatin is the understanding of it. Example, I did some testing (which others did as well) on fixing time, I found that 15 seconds did as good as 60, so the conclusion (thus far) is my tolerance for fixing is huge, same goes with exposure time, 25% is no big deal. But the combination (stack up) is very different. If you want to try several gelatin types and blooms then that would be worthwide.

Personally, I would like to see standardization involving diffraction efficency (how bright a holo is), clarity and noise. After all that is how a film, or a set up should be judged. Then variables can be set. Example, we all agree to use a 225 bloom gel, but it may or may not be the optimal gelatin for DCG. Or worst yet, how would we know? Success based on what? If I have a crappy set up and I say "hey this doesn't work" and John or Danny have a better set up and they say it is great, then what? And even that is subjective, is the result based on a photo? One taken in sun light, or 100 watt clear bulb? Then of coarse there the type of object and exposure time itself. What I have found difficult is the ability to make an exceptionally bright clear DCG every time, even from the same batch of film and same process. I'm not saying one is crap and the other is great, but that one holo that has that special quality which does not happen every time. It seems there is a set of conditions in which when everything (in combination) is just right it works. That is what seperates me from the masters 

So once again, I like the idea and would be willing to partake in any group activity but I have to wonder if it would result in a better DCG hologram. 

> **Seventh Son:** United we stand, divided we fall.

This by the way says a lot about the state of DCG IMO 

Lastly, I too get a bit fustrated with this soft science of DCG. I hope we can keep the dialog going in hopes we can see things from a different perspective. Perhaps this is the best idea in which if the group says it is then count me in for any assistance or through brainstorming something better come out. Thanks seventh for bring this subject up....

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Do not use fish gelatin, as Danny stated it is liquid at room temperature. Unless of course you want to play with that variable. I never tried it. Plus it is very dark, not very clear at all.

Though I never tried fish gelatin, I am pretty convinced there exist clear types - it's been used e.g. to make holographic AgX emulsions – fish gelatin is said to be very good at preventing grain growth.

What about these: [http://www.norlandprod.com/Fishdefault.tpl?cart=[cart](http://www.norlandprod.com/Fishdefault.tpl?cart=%5Bcart)]

Since fish gelatin doesn't gel, you'd have to add a hardening agent – maybe an aldehyde hardener. It would do the job without interfering with chrome hardening.

Another thing I've been wondering about related to DCG, involves denaturated gelatin (acylated or phtalated gelatin).

posts.author: Danny Bee
posts.content_md:
> **Seventh Son:** I only use bovine, but Emu sounds delicious!I'm scared to declare a bloom for this group. It seems like a fight waiting to happen.I've stated before that I like a high bloom, to resist ambient Rh...But that thread went nowhere fast.

altho the hi bloom is nicer (250-300) to resist ambient Rh, The 300 bloom is great for DYI process but for DCG its very hard to work with because all the lower molectular weight is filtered out. I have tried 300 bloom and got bright whites once, and was unable to repeat the process. Dinesh used 250 bloom, I have too but it takes a bit reworking the forumla and process, I do not recomended for beginner's, knox will come out with just as good as 250 bloom, but if your wanting to make dcg's for sale then 250 B type is a winner, but if your looking for brightness then the best way to make your holograms is h1 to h2 thats the way the pros do it
